name: Churches and Faith Organisations
blurb: Sermon prep, administration, and pastoral limits across hundreds of thousands of congregations, from Barna research and faith-tech platforms to Notre Dame ethics work.

points.desc: Census BTOS covers religious and civic organisations within its service-sector series; no better official measure exists yet, and this page says less rather than guessing.
points.name: Adoption is measured, not guessed

points.desc: The research firm's State of the Church work quantitatively tracks AI adoption, perception, and use among US congregations and ministry leaders - the closest thing to sector-wide survey data.
points.name: Barna Group runs the national studies

points.desc: Used by thousands of US churches, Gloo surveys faith leaders and builds AI tooling for ministry - a primary source for what deployment actually looks like in congregations.
points.name: Gloo is the sector's tech platform

points.desc: The interfaith nonprofit network brings scholars, technologists, and clergy together on the ethical deployment of AI in religious contexts.
points.name: AI and Faith convenes the ethics work

points.desc: The university's Institute for Ethics and the Common Good funds and tracks research on AI's impact on faith and religious life.
points.name: Notre Dame studies AI and human formation

points.desc: The Hartford Institute for Religion Research regularly surveys congregational trends and digital adoption across American places of worship.
points.name: Hartford surveys congregational technology

points.desc: Pew Research Center's Religion & Public Life work periodically measures how the public and clergy view technology and AI in religious spaces.
points.name: Pew measures public and clergy attitudes

summary: No single body tracks AI adoption across America's hundreds of thousands of congregations - coverage comes from research firms, faith-tech platforms, and academic institutes, and this page names them rather than pretending a census exists. Sermon research, translation, accessibility, and administration are the working uses; every tradition is writing its own guidance.

analysis.body:
Per the Census Bureau, the Business Trends and Outlook Survey first asked firms about AI use in September 2023, and the latest reading for Other services (NAICS 81, includes religious organizations) is 13.7% of firms answering yes to using AI in the last two weeks, up from 12.6% in the prior period. This is the official measure available, and the material here notes no better official measure exists yet.

Per Gloo, AI is a foundational capability across the Gloo platform to support mission effectiveness, preserve relational ministry and create practical value across the faith and flourishing ecosystem. Gloo AI delivers trusted, values-aligned models, developer tools, and benchmarks for faith-based organizations. Developers who build in Gloo AI Studio tap into a connected infrastructure of production environment tools, trusted content, and values-aligned AI models, with API-first support for inference, RAG, and assistant workflows and dynamic selection of the appropriate model for every request. The material gathered for this sector centers on sermon prep, administration, and pastoral limits across hundreds of thousands of congregations, drawing on Barna research, faith-tech platforms, and Notre Dame ethics work.

Vendor concentration in the material points to Gloo as the sector's tech platform, used by thousands of US churches, surveying faith leaders and building AI tooling for ministry. Barna Group runs the national studies on AI adoption, perception, and use among US congregations and ministry leaders, while the Hartford Institute for Religion Research surveys congregational technology and Pew Research Center measures public and clergy attitudes. No investment or revenue figures appear in the excerpts, so the money side is not quantified here.

The excerpts do not report quantified return on investment. Gloo describes creating practical value across the faith and flourishing ecosystem, but no ROI percentages or dollar outcomes are given.

Per AI and Faith, emerging issues around control and power, privacy, bias and discrimination, economic well-being, and even understanding what it means to be human are inherent to the ways AI is created and used in society, and the organization's mission is to equip people of faith to bring time-tested, faith-based values to the ethical AI conversation. AI and Faith also notes that for the 85 percent of the world’s population who claim a religious affiliation, these issues are deeply spiritual as well. Per Notre Dame, Meghan Sullivan says many workers in the industry talk very flippantly about job displacement and AI being able to do work faster and cheaper, and some are trying to transcend work. The Notre Dame Institute for Ethics and the Common Good promotes research and policy leadership in AI and other technology ethics, engaging stakeholders to examine real-world challenges and provide practical models and applied solutions for ethical technology design, development, and deployment, with a DELTA summit centering human formation and dignity in the AI transition. The excerpts describe a voluntary ethics and values posture rather than a regulatory one.

For a reader deciding whether to deploy, the official adoption figure is 13.7% in the latest period, up from 12.6% in the prior period, within Other services (NAICS 81, includes religious organizations). The sector has a dedicated platform in Gloo offering values-aligned models and developer tools. The ethics organizations represented here urge bringing faith-based values to AI, while Notre Dame warns about job displacement and human formation. The material supports a cautious, values-aligned approach rather than a rush to adopt.

https://ethics.nd.edu/.brief: The Notre Dame Institute for Ethics and the Common Good, directed by Meghan Sullivan, convenes a multidisciplinary community to tackle pressing ethical issues. It promotes interdisciplinary research, policy leadership, and practical models for ethical AI design, development, and deployment. The institute will host a second DELTA summit focused on human formation and dignity in the AI transition. Sullivan notes that many industry workers “talk very flippantly” about job displacement and AI’s speed and cost, while Lily Abadal observes that AI awareness is evolving.

https://www.barna.com/.brief: Barna Group, a Christian research organization, offers data and insights on faith, culture, and ministry trends. Their website hosts articles, reports, podcasts, courses, and services, including a free webcast replay that examines six trends shaping pastoral leadership. The site also promotes Barna’s latest research report, The State of Pastors, Volume 2, which explores how pastors navigate post-pandemic life and ministry across self-leadership, church leadership, and cultural leadership. A series of conversations features pastors Glenn Packiam, Rich Villodas, and Sharon Hodde Miller discussing leadership challenges and the health of the church. New Barna data indicates that one in three young adults is increasing church attendance, revealing who is leaning in and what they seek at church.

https://www.gloo.us/ai.brief: According to Gloo, its AI offering provides models, developer tools, and benchmarks that are aligned with the values of faith-based organizations. The company describes AI as a foundational capability across its platform, intended to support mission effectiveness, preserve relational ministry, and create practical value. Developers using Gloo AI Studio can access connected infrastructure including production environment tools, trusted content, and values-aligned models. The platform also offers API-first support for inference, RAG, and assistant workflows, with dynamic selection of the appropriate model for each request.

https://aiandfaith.org/.brief: AI and Faith is an organization that brings religious and faith-based perspectives to discussions about artificial intelligence ethics. The group argues that emerging AI issues—including control, privacy, bias, discrimination, and questions about human identity—are fundamentally moral questions, and that the world's religious traditions contain "ancient wisdom" relevant to how AI should be developed and used. The organization works to connect theologians, tech creators, researchers, and ethicists to integrate faith-based values into conversations about AI's ethical implications, aiming to introduce "humility and historicity into an industry that has often rejected them both."
